author: ch402
text: I suspect that a lot of “brilliant insights” are natural next steps from someone who has deep intimacy with a research topic. And that actually seems more profound.

author: ch402
text: As your intimacy with a research topic grows, your random thoughts about it become more interesting. Your thoughts in the shower or on a hike bounce against richer context. Your unconscious has more to work with. Your intuition deepens.

author: ch402
text: Research intimacy is also different from research taste. But it does feed into it, and I suspect it’s one of the key ingredients in beating the “research taste market.”

author: ch402
text: (A personal example: I’ve memorized hundreds of neurons in InceptionV1. I know how they behave, and I know how that behavior is built from earlier neurons. These seem like obscure facts, but they give me powerful, concrete examples to test ideas against.)

author: ch402
text: Research intimacy is different from theoretical knowledge. It involves internalizing information that hasn’t become part of the “scientific cannon” yet. Observations we don’t (yet) see as important, or haven’t (yet) digested. The ideas are raw.

author: ch402

Every approach to interpretability must somewhere turn an exponential into a polynomial.

Saliency: Local linearity allows exp(N_inp) -> N_inp

Circuits: Independent meaning of features turns exp(N_neurons) -> N_neurons

Small models: Limited size turns exp(N) => constant

author: ch402

author: ch402
text: @niru_m @vinayramasesh @Meaningness @michelteivel @moultano @zzznah Or, to look at another approach, how do saliency maps get around the curse of dimensionality? My steal man would be that the model is locally linear, so it's dynamics can be understood in terms of O(n) parameters locally.

author: ch402
text:
@niru_m @vinayramasesh @Meaningness @michelteivel @moultano Then, working with a @zzznah, we started seeing that many neurons seemed *independently understandable.*

This cuts through the curse of dimensionality. Instead of trying to understand exp(n) volume, you can independently understand n features.

author: ch402
text: @niru_m @vinayramasesh @Meaningness @michelteivel @moultano So, it worked in some cases because I studied models with low-dimensional representations, and the approach had no way to get around high-dimensional ones.

author: ch402
text: @niru_m @vinayramasesh @Meaningness @michelteivel @moultano I spent a while trying to generalize that using dimensionality reduction to understand the representations. author: ch402
text:
@prokraustinator And this is with the benefit of millions of dataset examples. My sense is that neuroscientists generally have far, far, far less.

A curve like shape might occur in 1 in 1000 receptive field exposures. A really clean curve in the right orientation might be more like in 10K.

author: ch402
text: @prokraustinator My experience is that teasing out a feature from dataset examples / natural stimuli is pretty brutal. How do you tell apart a dog eye vs dog head detector? A line vs boundary detector? Lots of features are highly correlated, but important to distinguish!

author: ch402
text: @prokraustinator I have no idea how we'd have sorted this out without feature visualization, or at least way more activation recordings than neuroscientists get. So neuroscience looks terribly hard from this perspective, even if neurons are meaningful!

author: ch402
text: @prokraustinator For example: InceptionV1 also has "divot detectors" (sharp point curves + lines), S-shape detectors, spiral detectors, line detectors and more which all fire a bit for curve stimuli. You could easily mistake them for bad curve detectors and then be very confused!

author: ch402
text: @prokraustinator Of course, we do also see "polysemantic" neurons that respond to multiple things. But (1) we can tell those apart from features that are doing things you might not have guessed; (2) we can see them be built ("superposition motif"); (3) I'm hopeful about finding a way around them.

author: ch402
text: @prokraustinator But we have tools like feature visualization (optimize through the model) and circuit analysis (look at how features are built from earlier features) which can help us infer what the feature is.

author: ch402
text: @prokraustinator You basically need to guess the right feature, then validate your hypothesis. If your guess is wrong but correlated, you'll see "noisy" features that don't quite seem right.

author: ch402
text: @prokraustinator My gut intuition -- which feels highly presumptuous to say -- is that features get murky in neuroscience because you have poor tools for sorting through they vast space of possible features.

author: ch402
text:

* ability to record arbitrarily many activations from all neurons without noise
* not just connectome, but weights
* ability to take gradients and optimize through the network

author: ch402

author: ch402
text:
@enolan @TacoCohen Let's imagine that rotational equivariance can cut parameter count by 2x in early vision (since there's also lots of features which aren't rotationally equivariant). And suppose that early vision is 20% of the model parameters.

That only gives a 10% parameter reduction.

author: ch402
text:
@enolan @TacoCohen Unfortunately, I don't think rotational equivariance has led to big wins on ImageNet (although it has helped on other tasks).

I think this is probably because we tend to see rotational equivariance significantly in early vision, and most model parameters are in late vision.

author: ch402
text: @enolan @TacoCohen We have some unpublished results visualizing equivariant neural networks, and they interact the way you'd expect with our equivariant features!

author: ch402
text: @enolan Yep! This is called "rotational equivariance" and there's some lovely work on encoding it (and other kinds of equivariance) into neural nets.  "Group Equivariant Neural Networks" by @TacoCohen  et al is a good starting point.
